segments.text: Hello and welcome to this week's edition of The Health Report with me, Norman Swan.
Today, time for a cold shower on the hype around medicinal cannabis.
Could Mars bars protect against obesity?
How obesity might not be the main step on the road to diabetes?
And the prospect that a blood test could tell you as much about your cancer as a biopsy?
There's been a remarkable turnaround in attitudes and legislation,
making it easier for people to take cannabis for medicinal purposes
and for the manufacture of cannabis products for medical uses.
But before we get carried away, an editorial in this week's Medical Journal of Australia warns that there are still significant gaps of knowledge which could put users at risk.
One of the co-authors of the editorial is Jennifer Martin, who's Professor of Clinical Pharmacology at the University of Newcastle.
And Jennifer was in our Newcastle studio last night.
Welcome to The Health Report.
Thank you. I'm pleased to be here.
Now, you talk about that you still require data.
We still don't know how effective, how safe and what the dose range is of these cannabis products.
That's correct.
We need more data.
But in addition, we also need a whole lot of other things to happen to make sure that we've actually ensured that patients are safe when they take cannabis.
So what are the worries?
Are there any signals about worries at the moment?
Well, I think there are a lot of concerns from prescribers, for example.
They have concerns as to how they would write a script for cannabis.
which type of cannabis would they prescribe?
How would they prefer to give it?
Is it given in a tablet or vaporised or smoked?
Or what is the recommendation for this particular patient
with this particular disease?
So I think there are concerns in the profession
about that aspect.
But I also think there are concerns in other areas
that maybe haven't had so much coverage,
such as the pharmacists,
who are going to have to be sure
they know how to store the cannabis
and all of the many different cannabis products.
They'll have to know how to look after them, what the security is around them,
how these things will be prescribed and what the follow-up for patients is.
Are there many products on the market yet?
I mean, what's around at the moment in Australia?
I know there's a lot on the market in the United States.
Yes, well, it's still an illegal substance, so that's the law.
But patients that I look after in the hospital are still able to access
different types of cannabis and cannabinoid from overseas.
Many grow it actually at home in the Hunter and make up their own products.
So there is quite a market out there of people that are already making or importing these therapeutic products to use themselves medicinally.
And have you seen anybody get into strife?
I have actually seen quite a few people in strife.
Most of them, actually, it's after the event.
And we're talking about how to manage, for example, their end-stage heart failure or their end-stage airways disease.
and they tell me about a bad experience they've had with cannabis
that's been prescribed, well, it's not prescribed,
that it's been brought to them by friends or family members
that are trying to be helpful.
And these are a particular population group that's often neglected in health,
such as the elderly and the elderly patients.
They describe quite significant cognitive and dysphoric reactions
after having cannabis.
And if you're importing cannabis from overseas, do we know what's in it?
We don't know what's in it.
That's correct.
I mean, there are places that you can get it tested.
For example, at Newcastle University,
we have the facilities to actually identify compounds
that are actually within the cannabinoid product.
Most of them are THC, which is the hallucinogenic compound,
and CBD, which is a cannabidiol,
which has been studied in epilepsy.
But there are a variety of other things that are in there
and that are added to it.
But that's correct, that people themselves
actually wouldn't know that.
I mean, some people would say,
and I can just see my mailbag tomorrow morning,
would say, well, you know,
these are just the old farts in the medical profession
trying to put up the barriers here.
And the best thing is just to smoke it.
All this medicine stuff is just a smoke screen
for pharmaceutical companies to make a lot of money.
That's exactly the feedback we get
from some members of the community as well.
They're a bit frustrated that the trials are taking so long.
You know, we haven't even started recruiting for some of them.
We don't have an active pharmacovigilance program out there.
And people are saying, well, why are you taking so long?
We all know this stuff is good.
Why don't you just get on with it?
And I think for recreational users, that's a reasonable argument
because we do have 2,000 years of information from people that use it recreationally.
But medicinal cannabis is used in a completely different group usually.
It's usually an older group.
They're usually pretty frail and comorbid.
That means they have lots of other medical problems.
There are lots and lots of drugs that might interact with the cannabis.
They might have difficulty inhaling a particular form of cannabis
because they lack the ability to inhale to get the active ingredients.
So I think the group that we're getting a lot of pressure from
is usually a recreational group.
And I think that what I'm concerned about as a medical practitioner
is more about protecting patients,
about making sure we actually don't give them something that's not safe
and actually potentially harm them.
And I actually think that's a reasonable,
I mean, I understand what you're saying about the paternalistic,
well, potentially implying that that's my way,
the paternalistic view of medicine,
but I do think we have a duty to protect patients as well.
And the other point I have is just that, you know,
there is a bit of research to suggest that some of these molecules
in the cannabis are actually quite helpful.
And if we get it wrong,
if we actually don't do the studies properly up front
and choose the wrong dose to study,
then we might think the cannabis...
You could spoil it.
We could spoil it.
And you never get a second chance to go back on that.
The energy's gone and people are onto something else.
So I think it was really not trying to be...
So go slow to get it right.
I think so.
And put the time and investment up front
to do the studies properly.
Jennifer, thanks very much for joining us.
Thank you.
Jennifer Martin is Professor of Clinical Pharmacology at the University of Newcastle.
And you're listening to The Health Report here on RN with me, Norman Swan.
Research published by Australian researchers in a prestigious international journal could
be interpreted as showing that eating confectionery protects against obesity.
Before you scream with delight and devour that bar of chocolate you've been eyeing in the
cupboard, there may be more to this story.
Earlier today, I spoke to two of the authors from the Murdoch Children's Research Institute
in Melbourne, Constantine Gasser and Professor Melissa Wake.
Melissa, what's the context for this study?
We've been very interested in obesity for a long time,
and I think it's becoming fairly clear that we've kind of hit a wall.
So after 15 years of really trying with education and lifestyle advice, etc.,
we haven't got very far.
And we really felt that we needed to go back a little bit
and really start to try and unpick some possible contributors
to obesity and healthy weight.
So that led to Constantine looking at this under-researched area.
which is the influence of confectionery on obesity.
So what did you do, Constantine?
We conducted a systematic review where we combined the results of 19 studies from around the world
to look at the association between confectionery consumption and overweight and obesity in children and adolescents.
Confectionery defined as what?
Candy and chocolates, but not including other types of sweets and desserts.
So we looked at confectionery and overweight and obesity and found, to our surprise, people with higher intakes of confectionery were actually slightly less likely to be overweight or obese.
Were the studies consistently in that direction?
So most of the studies were consistently in that direction.

So it's absolutely counterintuitive. And before we jump to the conclusion that we should all go out and chomp away at a Mars bar to protect ourselves against obesity, let's just assume a neutral position for the moment on this finding. If the finding were to be real, what sort of risk reduction on obesity did you get for confectionary use?
We compared children in the highest versus the lowest or a reference category of confectionary consumption in the studies,
and this differed across each of the studies.
But we found that overall the odds or likelihood of being overweight or obese was approximately 20% lower for children in the highest
compared to the lowest or a reference category of consumption.
And this was similar for both chocolate and non-chocolate confectionary.
So, Constantine, I can hear people rejoicing across the land.
do you think the finding is real?
Given that several studies have shown it,
and if we were talking about a more neutral topic,
you'd have said, oh, this is it,
you know, science sealed and delivered.
Factor X protects you against Y, no problem at all.
Well, we think that there are a number of possible reasons
for these findings.
Firstly, the possibility is that confectionery
may be a small aspect of the diet of these children and adolescents,
so it may not be contributing very much
to their daily energy or sugar intake.

For example, US data shows that confectionery or candy in the US comprises approximately 5% of their sugar intake compared to soft drinks and other sugar sweetened drinks, which comprise approximately 30%.

However, another reason for these findings is that overweight or obese children or adolescents or their parents may reduce their confectionery intake if they believe that it's an easy target in order to combat overweight or obesity.
so they may be reducing their intake of these foods.
So what you're saying is here that obese people have artificially lowered their confectionary rate
to try and control their obesity.
Yeah, to try and control obesity.
And therefore people who are thinner look artificially as if they're in a higher group.
Or they may have also underreported their intake of confectionary
if they believe that it was socially desirable to be consuming less confectionary
for health outcomes such as obesity.
And as a result, this may have been an explanation for some of the findings as well.
But it also could be real that, you know, once you've had a lolly or two or a bit of chocolate, your appetite for other sugar and other high calorie foods is lower.
And therefore, there's a trade off which is beneficial.

Yeah, possibly because of sugar being lower in kilojoules than fat, then this may have also been another possible explanation, meaning that they may have had an increased sense of fullness and consumed less of other foods.
but we do need to also consider the quantities that are being consumed
and also the detrimental effect of confectionery on other health outcomes
such as tooth decay, for example, because of the high sugar content.
So we're certainly not saying that we should be encouraging
high intakes of confectionery.
So, Melissa, you were hoping to eliminate the literature on obesity and diet
and all you succeeded in doing is confusing it even more.
Well, we think that we have come up with a really interesting finding.
It does seem likely that confectionary consumption is a fairly small part of children's food intake today.
We think that the culprits for obesity are likely to be too much food,
so large servings, uncontrolled snacks, second helpings, etc.
And also the sorts of foods that kids are predominantly eating sugary drinks,
but also foods that are high in fat and salt and sugar and processed carbohydrates
and large in terms of portion size.
So Health Report listeners across the land, and indeed across the world,
since we've got Canadian listeners, are looking in their cupboard hungrily at that bar of chocolate.
What should they do with it, Melissa Week?
Well, first they should make sure that it's dark chocolate.
They should encourage children to eat sparingly.
Certainly we know that dark chocolate does actually have some health benefits.
It does increase satiety.
It's quite hard to overindulge in dark chocolate.
And its high flavonoid content has been shown to have health benefits such as lower blood pressure.
So I would say keep an open mind.
Eat sparingly.
And if your child does eat confectionery, steer them towards something that does have ancillary health benefits.
Thank you both very much indeed for joining us on The Health Report.
It's a pleasure.
Thanks, Norbert.
Melissa Wake and Constantine Gasser at the Murdoch Children's Research Institute in Melbourne.
Speaking of sugar and obesity, there are about a million people with diabetes in Australia,
which includes around 130,000 with what's called type 1.
That's the insulin dependent form and not related to obesity necessarily.
We're among the highest prevalence nations in the world.
And one of the problems with diabetes that doesn't get much attention is the risk of hypoglycemia,
dangerously low levels of blood sugar.
And worryingly, some people with diabetes lose their ability to recognise when their blood sugar is plummeting.
And one answer may be reteaching people to become scared.
Our World Authority on Hypoglycemia was in Melbourne a few days ago, which is where I caught up with her.
And as you'll also hear, Professor Stephanie Emile of King's College London also has fascinating findings on which comes first in type 2 diabetes, obesity or problems with insulin.
And also surprising side effects of obesity surgery.
But let's start with hypoglycemia.
Hypoglycemic attack is never pleasant.
For most people, they are what we call mild, but the patient may not feel them as mild
because what happens is the blood sugar goes low,
they have a stress response which is symptomatic so it feels unpleasant,
but they also know what's happening so they eat something and it stops.
The problem is that sometimes, particularly in people who've lost the ability to feel their hypoglycemia like that,
the first thing that happens is confusion and cognitive impairment,
so they never get the opportunity to treat themselves.
The blood glucose goes on falling.
They become confused.
They may behave in an embarrassing or abnormal way
and they may get into loss of consciousness and seizure.
And so those severe hypoglycemic attacks
are obviously really very distressing and very unpleasant.
And that's what you're trying to prevent.
And if you've got lack of awareness,
is that really a major issue?
Yes, if you have too many minor hypos,
most people will then lose their ability to recognize them
and therefore they're much more prone to get a more severe hypo.
So if you've got type 1 diabetes and you don't recognize when your blood glucose dips below, let's say, about 3 mamol per litre.
Just to give people a sense of that, you've got diabetes when you're fasting blood sugars at 7, so 3 is at the lower end.
So under 3 and people start to notice, or other people start to notice in them a slight slowing of brain function.
And so if you're not noticing your own hypoglycemia at or around that sort of level,
then your risk for having one of these more severe episodes is much increased.
and if you're a type 1 diabetic so totally insulin dependent from the beginning then not being aware
of your hypoglycemia increases your risk of having a really bad episode by about sixfold and if you're
on insulin and you're a type 2 diabetic person then 17 fold it's a big risk factor. That's huge.
It is huge. Now you've been working on how you restore that awareness. Yes for a long time so
it's time we got there. You can restore it, you can restore it, this is going to sound very circular
but you can restore it by avoiding exposure to a plasma glucose, a blood glucose of under three.
Because basically what happens is the brain gets used to whatever you show it.
So if you show it a lot of blood glucoses of under three, it stops noticing and stops warning you about it.
And that can happen to people who are trying too hard to get their blood sugar down.
It can, and particularly people who are very, very committed to being really tightly controlled.
And healthcare professionals have been very good at telling people what glucose level they should be under.
we haven't been so good at making sure they realise that there's also a lower limit to normality
which they should remain over. So how do you get people to put a stop? The most successful thing
is to train people to manage their own insulin very physiologically so we call it flexible
intensified insulin therapy and that's hugely successful so that will restore awareness of
hypoglycemia to just under half of people who've lost awareness and it hugely reduces the risk of
severe hypoglycemia in the type 1 diabetic population. And in the type 2? We haven't done
so much in the type 2 because it's not such a big problem for the type 2s and that's partly because
most type 2s even when they need insulin do still have a bit of their own insulin and that seems to
be all they need to protect themselves from severe hypoglycemia. Also partly because there are now
new agents, new non-insulin agents available for people that don't carry the same hypoglycemia risk.
So if someone with type 2 is having hypoglycemia problems,
it's usually a matter of changing them on to one of these newer therapies
with lower hypoglycemic potential.
And if they are on insulin, then their problems are the same as the type 1s
and they can join that program.
And it's also been found that transplanting part of the pancreas can help too.
And also you've been looking at psychological therapies.
Yes, yes.
There is one step in between that,
which is the use of the newer technologies of glucose sensing and insulin delivery.
So these are the pumps and so on.
Sure.
because transplantation, it works, but it's obviously not suitable for everybody
and it's certainly not available to everybody.
We've been looking at psychological issues for a variety of reasons.
We looked at the brain's response to hypoglycemia in a very scientific way.
We did brain imaging, brain scanning,
and found that people who were unaware of their hypoglycemia
had very different brain responses to hypoglycemia,
including a failure to generate a message to themselves
that this was something really unpleasant that they should avoid at all costs.
So they had a low stress response?
They had a low stress response, so they didn't have the stress response, they didn't have the symptoms.
We expected that because they were unaware.
What we didn't expect was that they had different responses of the brain areas that tell us we're having fun, the reward areas.
And instead of turning those off and really knowing that this was unpleasant, they weren't doing that.
And some of them were even activating those areas in the opposite direction.
Is that because of the sort of person they were or because of the diabetes?
Well, that's an extremely good question.
We're testing that at the moment. We think it's just part of the whole syndrome of having induced a tolerance, if you like, of hypoglycemia because you've been exposed to it too often.
But it is possible that this particular part of the response in what we call the frontal areas of the brain, that might be genetically programmed and individual.
So it may be that these people are programmed to respond to a stress in a particular way that makes them more vulnerable to developing this whole problem of unawareness.
So it's not that we don't know.
Absolutely, we need to teach them to become scared because if you don't feel something,
it's not surprising that you don't worry about it.
But if we can teach them to become scared, they will then be able to access all the other information they've been given
that they should have been able to use before to help them avoid hypoglycemia.
Now your group has also been doing some fascinating research into obesity, diabetes, insulin,
because you reckon that insulin is actually a neurotransmitter. It affects brain function.
Yes, well, we're not the only people that reckon that, but certainly we have a bit of evidence of that in the particular area of appetite control,
which is obviously of great interest to us because of the worries about the number of people who are becoming insulin resistant, obese and getting type 2 diabetes.
So you've flipped it on your head because you actually think for some people what comes first in the pathway to diabetes is not obesity, but it actually is an insulin problem.
We have now some evidence for that. They've always been very tightly linked. So people know that not for everybody, but for most people who are obese, they're insulin resistant.
Meaning insulin doesn't work as well.
Doesn't work very well, exactly. And most people with type 2 are also insulin resistant.
And so we've never really known which comes first.
But we very recently done another brain imaging study, in fact, where we took people who were insulin resistant.
So they had very high insulin levels in order to control their blood glucoses.
so they've got normal glucose they're not diabetic but they're using a lot of insulin or making a lot
of insulin in order to achieve that and nor were they obese most of them weren't even overweight
so they were apparently completely healthy people in whom the only pathology we could find was that
they were making more insulin to maintain normality than someone who's more insulin sensitive and what
we did was to compare their brain's response to eating with people who were completely insulin
sensitive. And we found some significant differences, strangely enough, again, in these
areas of the brain that control appetite and pleasure, and the areas of the brain also that
inhibit our sort of basic instincts. So obviously the natural instinct of an animal like man is to
eat something, and we have frontal cortical control of that so that we don't just go on
eating forever. And the front parts of our brain control our ability to stop eating and our ability
not to eat again if we're not hungry. And those brain areas appear to function differently in
people who are not obese and not diabetic, but who are insulin resistant. Now we know those people
are at high risk for getting obesity and diabetes. And so it looks to us as though the insulin
resistance comes first. And it may be that in altering the way the brain responds to food and
alters the person's relationship to food, that may be why those people then go on to develop obesity
and diabetes. So how do you know that you're insulin resistant if you're not fat?
What we did was look for people who were at high risk for being insulin resistant. So we looked
for family members of people who had type 2 diabetes. And you've also found that with
bariatric surgery, people's behaviour changes. There's something hormonal that goes on.
There is indeed. So we've known for a long time that bariatric surgery doesn't just change
how much you eat, it also changes what you eat and your interest in eating.
Just to tell us more about that.
There are different forms of bariatric surgery,
but the one that is probably most successful in weight control and improving diabetes
is something called gastric bypass.
It's a fairly major procedure, but it removes the stomach
and it bypasses the very first part of the small intestine,
so the food goes straight from the gullet straight into the rest of the small intestine.
It's called Roux-en-Y, is the other thing?
It is indeed called Roux-en-Y, and it's very successful.
and we know that when that happens to you it doesn't just cause weight loss because of restricting the amount you can eat physically.
It's not malabsorptive but it changes your appetite control, it changes your taste for food
and it seems to change the things you enjoy eating in a more healthy direction.
So we looked at people who had had that operation and who were weight stable after it
and we again did some brain imaging studies looking at how their brains responded to food intake
and we found that their brains responded differently from the matched controls who were equally obese but hadn't had surgery.
And in some brain areas, the surgery appeared to normalise what was an abnormal response in the obese individual
and in other brain areas, it seemed to exaggerate or even invert the normal response
but all in ways that would be expected to help the brain better control your food intake.
It's absolutely astounding because what's happening in the gut is having an effect on the brain.
Yes, indeed. And there's a lot more knowledge about that now because we understand a lot more about the signals that the gut generates when you eat something.
So the gut makes a series of proteins that go to the brain and say, this person has eaten.
And that means you will stop eating because that creates a signal that tells you to stop eating.
And some of those signals also control the length of time before you feel you need to eat again.
And your food preference.
And your food preference, absolutely.
It's all about appetite control and pleasure and what seems good to you.
And they're also taking more exercise.
I'm not sure how well that's been documented.
We certainly saw that in a recent very small study we did
using a little device that mimics one of the effects of the Roux-en-Y,
which is to exclude the duodenum, the upper part of the small intestine.
And with that device, where food didn't touch the top part of the small intestine
as it went through to the bowel, this is purely anecdotal,
not very scientific, but anecdotally, those people not only changed what they ate and how
much they ate, they started to exercise. So that needs investigating because that's very exciting.
Stephanie Emile is Professor of Diabetic Medicine at King's College London.
One of the hot areas in cancer research at the moment is the idea of the liquid biopsy.
Sounds goopy, I know, but it's the hope that if you look closely enough at a person's blood,
there may be a lot it can tell you, either about whether they have cancer to begin with
or how effective a treatment might be.
Francesco Grignani is professor of pathology at the University of Perugia.
When you have an early stage of lung cancer,
you actually do not know whether this cancer will relapse after surgery
or if the patient is cured by surgery.
At the moment, very few parameters to predict
what will happen in the future for these patients.
And we are looking for markers which would help
in predicting the outcome of these patients,
and we actually think that we can find these parameters in the blood of the patients.
So simply a blood test?
For the patient, it's just a blood test.
And what you're particularly looking at are lung cancers?
We are studying lung cancer in our lab,
but many labs all over the world are actually studying,
with the same approach, different types of cancers,
for which a prognosis can be made by drawing a little bit of blood
and measuring new molecular parameters in the blood.
It's complicated, but these so-called cancer markers or biomarkers in the blood
are often fragments of RNA called micro-RNAs.
One of the key functions of RNA is to read off the genetic code held on the DNA,
on our chromosomes, and transport the messages to factories within the cell,
which will then read the RNA and manufacture the proteins that the code is designed to produce.
In cancer, there are abnormal RNAs from the pathological processes inside cancer cells,
and they can spill out from the cells into the blood.
Francesco Grignani again.
So measuring these RNAs could help us in predicting what happens in a cancer patient.
You talk about a simple blood test, but then presumably once it gets to that,
that gets fairly complicated to actually work out what these RNAs are.
Of course, for the patient it's a blood test, but for us it's very complicated.
But the techniques are developing, so we are now able to collect many, many clinical samples
and perform good analysis in very large numbers of patients to reach significant results.
So what you've done is you've taken people with relatively early stage lung cancer
and measured these RNAs, and what have you found?
Well, we found that a certain combination of these RNAs suggests that the patient will relapse.
And even a certain combination suggests that the patient will die of his disease.
On the other hand, if you do not have this combination of RNAs, you are probably cured.
So you will not need any further therapy.
Which is quite remarkable. And is this in smoking-related lung cancer or non-smoking-related lung cancer?
This is actually even more solid in non-smoking-related lung cancer.
For smoking-related cancers, several groups are working on predicting the onset of the cancer
before it can be seen in imaging techniques
by looking at the blood of the people who are at risk of lung cancer.
One of the problems with blood tests is reliability.
How accurate is the testing for these RNAs at the moment
and how long before it becomes so standardized that you can really do it reliably?
The way you get the blood and where you store the blood is standardized.
And probably in a few years will be routine.
And the price? Because cost in Italy and in Australia is really important.
Now, this is costly, but identifying a few of these RNAs...
So it's cheaper when you...
It's much cheaper if you measure three, four RNAs instead of measuring a few hundred RNAs.
The other question that patients will have is, well, it's fine telling me, well, I don't want to hear it,
but it's fine telling me that I'm going to relapse or I might even die.
But are there any treatment insights that you can get from these RNAs?
Do they relate to the increasing number of genetic mutations which tell you that a certain drug might work on your cancer?
This is something we are looking at right now, and hopefully we will find the correlation that we are looking for,
for a better treatment of the cancer.
Francesco Grignani is Professor of Pathology
at the University of Perugia
and you've been listening to The Health Report
with me, Norman Swan.
Look forward to your company next week.
